entries.text: That attacking is a matter of temperament. The classical position is that it is a consequence of an advantage you already hold.
That an exposed king is losing.
That pushing pawns at the king is an attack. Without pieces to follow, it is a structural concession.
An attack without a positional advantage generally fails; this is the doctrine's core and it is a genuine constraint, not encouragement.
A wing attack can be refuted by a central counter-blow — the standard antidote.
Trading queens usually ends an attack, so the defender's simplest defence is often to seek that trade.
Damaged pawn cover is not decisive by itself. It matters in proportion to the attacking force that remains.
Two checks is not an attack. The repository's `kingAttack` tag fires on checks >= 2 or mate, which is a proxy for puzzle classification and NOT a definition of the concept.
An exposed king is not automatically under attack — with the attacking pieces traded off, an exposed king is often just an active one. This is a registered false-positive case.
Advancing pawns at a king is not an attack unless pieces can follow into the lines that open.
attack because the king looks exposed
always attack
That pushing pawns at the king is an attack. It is a way of making a road; without pieces it is a weakness.
That storms are always double-edged. With opposite-side castling they cost the attacker nothing.
With same-side castling the storm is a concession first and an attack second.
A central counter-blow refutes a premature storm — the standard antidote.
Against an intact shield with no hook, the storm may never force a file open at all.
Advancing pawns at a king is not an attack unless pieces can follow. Without that, it is a structural concession.
With same-side castling the same moves that attack also expose, and this is the commonest way a storm rebounds.
Counting the storm's speed without counting the defender's central break is how these positions are misjudged.
pushing pawns is an attack
That any distraction is equally damaging. Timing and novelty decide.
That the danger is forgetting individual pieces. The evidence points at disruption of pattern matching during encoding.
Interference after a position is encoded is comparatively harmless, which is the opposite of what the folklore suggests.
Static irrelevant information is tolerated by masters; only changing information disrupts.
A fact about the player and the interface, not about the position or any move.
The finding is specifically about visual and attention-demanding interference during encoding. Generalising it to 'distraction is bad' loses the whole result, which is that timing decides.
distraction is always equally bad
That blindfold players hold a photographic image of the board. This was the hypothesis the first study set out to confirm and had to abandon.
That blindfold chess is a feat of raw memory. Masters have no advantage at all on randomly arranged positions; the advantage is in meaningful structure.
That it requires an exceptional gift. The evidence points at accumulated chess knowledge rather than unusual memory.
Individual players differ in how much visual quality they report, and Fine noted that a blank board helped some players and hindered him.
The finding concerns skilled players; it does not describe how a novice attempts the task.
This is a fact about the player, not about the position. It must never be attached to a move as though it explained one.
It describes SKILLED players. A beginner attempting blindfold play may well be trying to hold a literal picture, which is part of why it is so hard for them.
picture the board
photographic memory
visualise the scene
That blindfold play requires a rare gift. The evidence points at accumulated knowledge and trainable sub-skills.
That one should begin by attempting a whole blindfold game. The instructional consensus is the reverse.
Blindfold play is an advanced application, not a starting point; the drills come first.
Fine reported that a blank board was a hindrance rather than a help to him, while other players found it useful - individual variation is real.
This describes a player's skill, not a position. It cannot be attached to a move.
The transfer claim - that these drills raise playing strength - is not evidenced and must not be repeated as fact.
blindfold chess requires a gift
That masters have better memories. On random positions they do not.
That a chunk is a fixed opening pattern. It is any group of pieces bound by chess relations.
The advantage does not extend to randomly arranged positions, which is the finding that makes the theory testable.
Chunking alone underestimates how fast experts encode into long-term memory, which is why template theory was needed.
A fact about players, not positions. It cannot be reported as a feature of a move.
Chunking explains recall of MEANINGFUL positions only. The master advantage is zero on random arrangements, and claiming otherwise inverts the central finding.
masters have better memories
That the rule of the square is about distance. It is about the square, and about whose move it is.
That a knight can lose a tempo. It cannot: every knight move changes square colour, so returning takes an even number of moves.
The rule of the square fails if the pawn's path is blocked, if it can be supported by its own king, or if the defending king's route is obstructed.

The rule of the square must be applied with the side to move in hand. This base holds a tablebase-proven pair where the identical position is a draw or a mate in 23 depending only on whose turn it is.
The rule of the square assumes a clear path: another pawn, or a king in the way, breaks it.
Colour-boundedness is a fact about bishops, not a claim that a bishop is limited — it is also why the pair is worth more than two of anything else.
the king is slow
count the distance to the pawn
That the point values are facts. They are averages, and their authors disagree.
That being ahead on material means being better. A proven draw in this base is a bishop and pawn up.
That a bishop is worth more than a knight. That is one position in a live dispute, not a settled value.
Fortresses and wrong-coloured-bishop draws are proven counterexamples to the count.
With all pawns on one wing the knight is generally stronger than the bishop, reversing the usual ordering.
The exchange (rook for minor) is given up often enough that treating it as a fixed +2 is a mistake.
Counting material is not evaluating a position. This base holds a PROVEN DRAW a bishop and a pawn up.
The values are disputed among their own authorities, and the bishop-versus-knight disagreement is a full half-pawn wide.
The pair bonus attaches to having two bishops, not to each bishop. Reporting a lone bishop as worth more than a knight asserts the disputed claim.
a bishop is worth more than a knight
the piece values are
That a rook belongs on any open file. It belongs on one with a square to invade.
That diagonals are secondary to files. The long diagonals are the longest lines on the board.
Knights ignore lines entirely, which is what makes them the right piece for closed positions.
A line being open is a fact; its being useful is not. This base holds a tested position where an open file with a rook of each colour on it is worth exactly nothing.
diagonals are less important than files
That stronger players calculate more deeply and widely. De Groot found they do not search more, and may search less.
That calculation can replace judgement. A variation is worth only what the position at its end is worth.
That calculating further is always better. Ideas at the start of a line matter more than refinements at the end.
Many positions are decided by judgement and require almost no calculation.
In defence the emphasis shifts: pare the candidates down harder and examine the most critical first, since there is little point exploring suspect lines.
A description of how a player thinks, not a feature of the position. It cannot be offered as the reason a move is good.
That a move requires calculation is not evidence that it is correct.
strong players calculate deeper
That Kotov's tree describes how strong players actually think. It does not, on the testimony of several grandmasters including one who checked Kotov's own analysis.
That revisiting a line is a lack of discipline. It is how the comparison between lines is made, and the ideas found in one line frequently belong in another.
That a longer candidate list is better. Breadth is for generating; the work is done by going deep on the critical one.
Positions with one forced line need no list; the tree is a single branch.
Nunn's goal-seeking case: moves that only make sense as part of a larger operation will not appear in any candidate list, and must be found another way.
Tisdall argues the candidate list should not be the primary task at all, and that leaning on an instinctive first choice engages intuition and starts the abstract assessment.
This is a technique for the player, not a property of the position, and must never be presented as an explanation of why a move is good.
The one-pass tree must not be taught as current best practice. Nunn, Dvoretsky, Tisdall and Leitao all reject it, and this base records the rejection as the consensus.

Some strong moves are unreachable by candidate generation at all. Nunn's example is a move that 'makes absolutely no sense except as part of the whole tactical operation' and so never enters a candidate list.
analyse each line only once
never go back in a variation
That a plan is a sequence of moves. The opponent gets to move too; a plan is an objective and an arrangement.
That having any plan beats having none. A bad plan pursued rigidly is worse than responding to the position.
That abandoning a plan is weakness. Recognising that circumstances changed is a skill in itself.
Forcing positions need calculation, not planning.
Shereshevsky's 'thinking in schemes' inverts the usual order in endgames: decide the target arrangement first, then find the route to it.
A plan that names nothing cannot be verified, followed or abandoned, and is not a plan.
A plan that ignores the opponent's counterplay is the standard way good-looking moves lose games.
This system cannot know a player's plan and must not attribute one to a move without evidence.
improve my position
create pressure
a plan is a series of moves
That any piece will do. The choice of blockader is most of the concept.
That blockading is free. It commits a piece, and Nimzowitsch says so.
A blockade that ties down a piece needed elsewhere is a liability.
Blockading with a heavy piece is expensive and usually temporary.
The pawn must not be allowed too far forward before the blockade is established — Nimzowitsch's own caveat.
A piece standing in front of a pawn is not necessarily blockading it usefully. The test is whether the piece keeps its powers there — a queen on a blockading square is doing a knight's chore.
A blockade becomes a weakness when it ties down a piece needed elsewhere, which is the standard cost and is easy to omit.
A pawn stopped by an enemy PAWN is a ram, not a blockade, and no piece is being spent.
blockade with anything
That defence means making passive moves and waiting. It is an active discipline with its own techniques.
That a worse position should be simplified. That is right when the position is holdable and wrong when it is lost.
That attacks succeed because attack is stronger than defence. The classical claim is the reverse: attacks from equal positions should fail, and succeed largely because defence is played badly.
Passive defence is sometimes objectively correct, particularly where a known drawing set-up requires it - Polugaevsky gives an example where the outwardly more active move loses.
Against a lost position, objectively bad moves that complicate can be the best practical choice.
Polugaevsky is explicit that modern success rests on offensive play, and that seeking defence contrary to the position's demands is as punishable as any other error.
Defence is not passivity. Recommending a passive move because a position is worse is the commonest defensive error, not a defensive principle.
The simplify-versus-complicate advice is genuinely contradictory in the sources and must not be reported as settled. Which applies depends on whether the position is holdable or lost.
A concession that was not forced is not a defensive move. Conceding early and conceding more than necessary are the two ways defences collapse.
defence means waiting
always simplify when worse
That overprotection is generally good practice. It is a named historical idea with limited modern support.
That more defenders is safer. Beyond what a concrete line needs, extra defenders are usually idle pieces.
Defending an unattacked point is usually a waste of time, and modern practice says so.
Engines defend exactly as much as a line requires.
Counting defenders is mechanical and says nothing. Overprotection is a CLAIM that the extra defence is worthwhile, and that claim is often false.
This is the idea most likely to license bad advice. Do not report it unless the overprotecting pieces are demonstrably well placed for other reasons as well.
always overprotect the centre
That prophylaxis means passive or defensive play. Nimzowitsch explicitly says it is neither attack nor defence.
That it only concerns the opponent. He distinguishes external from internal prophylaxis, the latter aimed at one's own position.
That it is a modern refinement. It is his stated central conception of positional play, from 1925.
Prevention has a cost. If the opponent's idea was not dangerous, the tempo is simply lost.
In sharp positions, speed can outweigh prevention — a prophylactic move in a race loses the race.
Nimzowitsch's ranking of prophylaxis above accumulation is a claim about emphasis and was polemical; the two are complementary.
Any quiet move can be called prophylactic after the fact. The claim requires naming the specific idea prevented — if you cannot name it, the move was just quiet.
Preventing a threat that does not exist is not prophylaxis, it is a wasted move.
This is not detectable from a static position. It is a property of what the move DENIES, which requires knowing what the opponent intended.
prophylaxis means playing passively
any quiet move is prophylactic
That restraint is defensive. Nimzowitsch treats it as the first stage of an attacking plan.
That it is the same as the blockade. The blockade is restraint made permanent by a piece.
Restraining an advance the opponent did not want is a wasted move.
In sharp positions speed beats restraint.
Restraint is not the same as passivity. It reduces the opponent's options; a passive move merely fails to increase yours.
Like prophylaxis, it is easy to assert after the fact about any quiet move. Name the advance being prevented.
restraint is passive play
That controlling the centre means putting pawns there.
That the hypermoderns thought the centre was unimportant — they thought it was too important to commit to early.
That one school won. Textbooks treat hypermodernism as an extension of classical theory, not a replacement.
Occupying the centre is not always right — an unsupported pawn centre is a target, which is the hypermodern case.
Ceding the centre is not always right either — against proper support it just loses space.
In the endgame the logic inverts: the centre matters for king activity rather than for restriction.
Counting pawns on central squares measures occupation, not control. A fianchettoed bishop controls e4 without standing anywhere near it.
A big pawn centre is not automatically an advantage. Whether it is an asset or a target is a question of timing and support, and that cannot be read off the structure.
Central pieces are only strong while they cannot be kicked; a piece on a central square a pawn can attack is visiting.

A rook or queen whose line to a central square runs through one of its own men counts as an attacker and should not be read as a piece fighting for the square. The move-based arm measures pawns and minors for this reason.
always occupy the centre with pawns
the centre does not matter
That the initiative is the same as being better. A worse position can hold the initiative, and often that is the only reason it survives.
That checks and captures create an initiative. They create forcing moves, which is not the same thing.
That it is White's by right.
It expires. An initiative that is not converted into something permanent is worth nothing afterwards.
A series of forcing moves is not an initiative if the replies help the opponent.
Black can hold it. It is not White's by right of the first move.
A series of checks is not an initiative. If the opponent's forced replies improve their position, you are helping them.
Having more active pieces is not the same as having the initiative — the test is whether they must answer you.
The initiative is invisible to a static feature scan, so it cannot be detected from the board alone; it is a property of the sequence.
the initiative means you are better
White always has the initiative
That the rules are rules. They are defaults for players who cannot yet judge the exception.
That moving a piece twice is a mistake.
That the queen must stay home until move 10.
That 'the opening' ends at a fixed move number. It ends when the pieces are developed.
That moving the same piece twice in the opening is an error. In the Ruy Lopez it is the best move, measured at +0.42 against +0.08 for the alternative.
Moving a piece twice to capture, to escape, or to reach a decisively better square.
Early queen sorties that cannot be harassed — the Scandinavian's ...Qa5 is theory, not an error.
Delaying castling deliberately when the centre is closed, or when castling would walk into a prepared attack.
Hypermodern openings that decline to occupy the centre at all and invite overextension instead.

REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: moving the same piece twice is not automatically wrong. Capturing, escaping and reaching a much better square all justify it, and this is the brief's own illustration of tactics overriding a principle.

REGISTERED FALSE POSITIVE: early queen development is not automatically wrong — the objection is that the queen can be harassed WITH TEMPO, so where no such harassment exists the objection does not apply.
Detecting a rule violation is easy and says almost nothing. Only the absence of a concrete justification makes it a criticism.
'The opening' has no fixed end. Applying opening rules at move 15 of a closed position is a category error.
A piece moving twice is not evidence of a mistake. Proven counterexample: 4.Ba4 in the Ruy Lopez is best by 0.34 over any move that leaves the bishop alone.
never move the same piece twice
never bring the queen out early
That more space is simply better. It is better if you can enter.
That advancing pawns gains space safely. It also fixes them and leaves holes behind them.
Space with no way in is worth little.
Space bought by overextension is a liability — the hypermodern critique.
The cramped side exchanging pieces is the standard and effective antidote.
Counting controlled squares is mechanical and over-reports. Space with no entry point wins nothing.
Advanced pawns are not automatically a space advantage — they may simply be weak and fixed.
The cramped side's standard remedy is exchanging, so a space advantage that cannot prevent trades is temporary.
more space is always better
That a tempo is worth a third of a pawn. It has no fixed value.
That gaining tempi is always good — driving an enemy piece to a better square costs you more than it gains.
That tempo and initiative are the same thing.
'Losing a tempo' is a virtue in the endgame, where triangulation aims at exactly that.
A tempo has no fixed value; the three-tempi-per-pawn heuristic is an opening rule of thumb only.
Moving the same piece twice is not automatically a lost tempo.
Chasing a piece with a threat it WANTED to answer is not gaining a tempo — the classic case is driving a piece to a better square with an attack.
Counting tempi in a closed position, where they may be worth nothing.
Treating 'moved the same piece twice' as automatically a lost tempo. This is a registered false-positive case: a capture, an escape, or a decisively better square all justify it.
a tempo is worth a third of a pawn
That it is a more complicated version of the opposition. It is the general theory; the opposition is its simplest case.
That it applies broadly. It applies to blocked king-and-pawn endings and almost nowhere else.
Any spare pawn tempo dissolves the correspondence.
Where opposition suffices, the extra machinery adds nothing.
The framework is only needed where opposition fails. Invoking it where simple opposition answers the question is unhelpful precision.
Correspondences break the moment a pawn tempo becomes available.
This is an expert-level tool. Reporting it to a player who has not yet mastered the opposition explains nothing.
corresponding squares are just the opposition
That endgames are simple because few pieces remain. They are the most exact phase, which is the opposite of forgiving.
That trading into an endgame is safe when ahead. Which endgame is reached decides, and several are proven draws a piece down.
Do not hurry does not apply against a concrete threat or in a race, where a single tempo decides.
Centralisation of the king has documented failures in rook endings, recorded on its own concept.
Simplification, the other common endgame reflex, can convert a proven win into a proven draw - this base holds tablebase proofs of exactly that.
The boundary is not sharp. A queenless position with many pieces may still be a middlegame, and treating it as an endgame is how kings get mated.
These are organising ideas, not a substitute for calculation. Every one of them has recorded exceptions, several proven by tablebase in this base.
endgames are simple
always trade when ahead
That a fortress is any stubborn defence. It is the impossibility of progress.
That the engine bar settles it. This is the clearest case where it does not.
That being material down means losing. A fortress makes the material count irrelevant.
A fortress that can be broken by a sacrifice was never a fortress.
Many apparent fortresses fail to zugzwang once the defender's waiting moves run out.
Within tablebase range the question is not a judgement at all — look it up.
A position that is merely HARD to break is not a fortress. The test is that no progress is possible at all, and that is a strong claim.
Claiming a fortress on the basis of an engine evaluation being stuck is backwards — engines misjudge these in BOTH directions.
A defender with a limited number of waiting moves does not have a fortress; they have a position that loses to zugzwang.
The commonest error is the reverse one: declaring a real fortress lost because the material count says so.
the engine says +3 so it is winning
That the opposition is the goal. The key square is the goal; the opposition is a means.
That key squares are the same for every pawn. They depend on the pawn's rank and file.
Rook pawns have their own, much more restrictive key squares and are often drawn.
Reaching a key square by the direct route is sometimes impossible while a route around the pawn works.
Key squares are only meaningful in king-and-pawn endings. Reporting them with pieces on the board is a category error.
For a rook pawn the usual rules do not apply and the ending is frequently drawn regardless.
Reaching a key square is the goal; taking the opposition is only one way of getting there and is sometimes the wrong one.
always take the opposition
That the king should be kept safe in the endgame as it is earlier. The change in the king's role is what defines the phase.
That centralisation is always correct. Its own advocate documents rook endings where it is not.
Rook endings, where the author of the principle records finding outright incorrect centralisation and attributes it to their concreteness and to the king's larger defensive role.
Positions where the king is still exposed to checks that gain the opponent tempi.
Races, where a centralising move may simply be too slow.

The single most important trap is rook endings, on the testimony of the principle's own advocate: Shereshevsky found centralisation there to be not merely untimely but sometimes simply wrong, and warns against automatic centralising moves.
A king moving towards the centre is not automatically doing the right thing; the move still has to survive checks. His example has 1...Ke5? losing to 2.Rd5+ while the retreat 1...Kc5! draws.
Centralisation with queens still on is a different matter entirely and this concept does not apply.
Never recommend centralising a king while the opponent has a queen, whatever the piece count says. The phase test in lib/features.js is material-based and can call a queens-on position an endgame.
always centralise the king
keep the king safe in the endgame
That a knight ending is a pawn ending. It is one for the purposes of several techniques and is not one when the knights start forking.
That knights are good blockaders and good chasers. They are excellent at the first and poor at the second.
Knight against knight and pawn is explicitly outside the principles: the standard reference says there are none operative for many such positions.
The knight is poor at catching a passed pawn, so the pawn-ending intuition about races does not transfer.
Rook pawns suit the knight badly.

Botvinnik's formula is a guide to which techniques transfer, not a claim that the ending IS a pawn ending. The knight's ability to fork and check reintroduces tempo, and knight against knight and pawn has no operative principles at all on the standard reference's own account.
A knight cannot lose a tempo, so triangulation and other tempo-losing methods that work with other pieces are unavailable to it.
a knight ending is a pawn ending (unqualified)
That the point count settles unbalanced endings. It is least reliable precisely here.
That two minor pieces automatically beat a rook. They do when coordinated and lose when they are not.
Fortresses defeat material reasoning entirely and are common in this class.
The bishop's statistical edge reverses when the pawns are all on one wing.
The point count is least reliable exactly here, and this is where people rely on it most. This base holds a proven draw a bishop and a pawn up.
The 60% figure for bishops over knights in endings is a population statistic and says nothing about a particular position.
This class is under-researched in this base, and confidence should stay low regardless of how clean the material description looks.
two minors beat a rook
count the material
That opposite-coloured bishops mean a draw. That is an endgame tendency, and the reverse is true in the middlegame.
That an extra pawn or two settles it. Two extra pawns frequently fail to win.
That a bad bishop is bad here. For the defender it is the correct setup.
The drawish rule is an endgame rule. With queens and rooks on, opposite bishops favour the attacker.
Three files of separation between passed pawns usually wins despite the bishops.
A wrong rook pawn draws regardless of how far apart or how advanced the pawns are.
The defender's best practice is the opposite of normal: make your bishop bad on purpose.

The drawish reputation is an ENDGAME fact. In the middlegame with heavy pieces on, opposite-coloured bishops favour the attacker, because the bishop operates where the defender's cannot answer. Announcing 'opposite bishops, drawn' with queens on the board is the standard error.
Detecting the material is trivial; whether a blockade is achievable is not.
Two extra pawns are often not enough — but three files of separation often are. The count of pawns is the wrong variable; their separation and the blockade are the right ones.
opposite bishops means a draw
That having the opposition means it is your move. It means the opposite — the side NOT to move has it.
That taking the opposition is always right.
That it is a rule of thumb. In king-and-pawn endings it is provably exact.
Taking the opposition is not always best. Averbakh: it is a means to an end, and if it does not lead to a key square, marching the king there directly may be correct.
A spare pawn tempo neutralises it entirely.
In positions decided by a pawn race, king geometry may be irrelevant.
Kings facing each other is trivially detectable and means nothing outside endgames where king penetration decides.
Taking the opposition is not always correct. In some positions the king should ignore it and head for a key square directly — this is Averbakh's corrective and it is the standard error.
A spare pawn tempo makes the opposition irrelevant, since it can simply be handed back.
I have the opposition because it is my move
always take the opposition
That perpetual check is a rule of chess. It is not, and has not been for a long time.
That you can 'claim a perpetual'. You claim threefold repetition or the fifty-move rule.
That any long series of checks is a perpetual.
It is not a rule and cannot be claimed as one. The claimable rules are threefold repetition and the fifty-move rule.
For the side that stands better a perpetual is a failure, not a resource.
Other chess variants forbid it outright, so it is not a necessary feature of chess-like games.
A series of checks that merely delays the end is not a perpetual. The test is whether the position REPEATS, not whether checks are available.

The repo's detector is a proxy — two or more checks and a near-level final evaluation — which will also fire on a position that is simply drawn after some checks. Treat the tag as a candidate, not a finding.
Reporting a perpetual as a good outcome for the side that was winning inverts the meaning entirely.
draw by perpetual check (as a rule)
claim a perpetual
That an extra pawn should win. Queen endings convert less often than rook endings, which are themselves notoriously drawish.
That perpetual check is a lucky escape. It is the defender's standard plan and should be expected.
Where the defending king is exposed, the usual perpetual-check defence may fail and ordinary material logic returns.
Fortresses exist in queen endings and defeat material reasoning entirely.
Counting pawns is a poor guide here: an advanced passed pawn outweighs a numerical deficit, because a queen can escort it alone.
An extra pawn is much less often decisive than in a rook ending, and this class wins less frequently than the rook equivalent.
Reasoning from principle is weak in queen endings. Where the position is small enough for a tablebase, look it up.
an extra pawn wins
That an extra pawn wins a rook ending. A great many such positions are drawn, because of how many defensive constructions exist.
That the rook belongs behind the passed pawn. It often does, and this base holds a proof that as a general rule it is false.
That rook endings can be played on principle. They are the type most resistant to that.
Tarrasch's rule fails in the Vancura configuration, proven in this base.
King centralisation fails in some rook endings, on the testimony of the principle's own advocate.
Passive defence is sometimes correct, in defiance of the activity principle, when a known drawing set-up requires it.
This is the endgame type where general rules are least trustworthy, and this base holds proofs against three of them: Tarrasch's rule, king centralisation, and the value of a check.
A pawn advantage is much weaker evidence here than elsewhere, because the defensive constructions are so numerous.
Recognising the material as a rook ending says almost nothing. The concrete configuration decides.
the rook belongs behind the passed pawn
an extra pawn wins
That triangulation is the only way to lose a tempo. A spare pawn move is usually available and simpler.
That any king manoeuvre returning to the same square is triangulation. It must return the position with the OTHER side to move.
That a knight can do it.
A knight cannot triangulate — it cannot return to a square in an odd number of moves.
A spare pawn move does the same job more cheaply.
The textbook example does not require triangulation; several moves win and a direct one wins faster.

MEASURED: the standard textbook position for triangulation does not require it. Every king move wins there and a direct pawn move wins fastest. Do not report triangulation as necessary without checking that the alternatives fail.
A spare pawn tempo achieves the same thing more cheaply and is usually available.
A knight cannot triangulate; asserting it can is a geometric error.
you must triangulate here
That an extra bishop and pawn must win. Against the wrong rook pawn it is a dead draw.
That getting the king in front of the pawn draws, as it does with king and pawn alone. It does not.
That the engine evaluation can be trusted here. This is a documented evaluation blind spot.
A second pawn on a different file normally wins.
If the defending king cannot reach the corner in time, the attacker wins normally.
In the mirrored rook-versus-bishop cases the logic inverts: there the DEFENDER has the wrong bishop when it is the colour of the corner its king is confined to.

Being in front of the pawn is NOT enough, unlike king-and-pawn endings. The defending king must reach the corner or the square beside it — Mednis gives a position where the same setup wins with White to move and draws with Black to move.
A second pawn on a different file usually changes the verdict entirely.
The bishop's colour relative to the CORNER is what matters, not its current square.
an extra piece always wins
That zugzwang means having no good moves. It means every move is bad AND that being obliged to move is what causes it.
That Lasker or Nimzowitsch coined it. Lasker introduced it to English in 1905; the coinage is unestablished.
That it is a modern idea. The concept predates the word by over a thousand years.
A side with a spare tempo is not in zugzwang, however constrained it looks.
In the middlegame, with many pieces on, genuine zugzwang is rare — usually a bad position is just a bad position.
A position where the side to move is simply losing is not zugzwang. The test is whether having to MOVE is the cause — flip the side to move and see whether the result changes.
Being short of good moves is not zugzwang; every move must worsen the position.
In middlegames, apparent zugzwang is usually just a bad position.
zugzwang means no good moves
That advanced concepts are more useful. They are more dependent, which is a different thing and often makes them less usable.
